# Implementation & Coding Standards {#sec-goodcoding}

Good code is important; it is like good writing. If you read a story that is written incoherently, it takes much longer to read and understand, if you can understand it at all. The problem with bad code is that it can actually work and produce the correct result. If the result is all that counts, you might get lured into the swamp of bad code. If you, your colleague, or your future self has to make changes to the code, that swamp can turn out to be a nightmare. The code is hard to understand, hard to maintain, and hard to extend or reuse. This leads to frustration, errors, and wasted time.

It takes time to learn how to write good, concise, and easy-to-understand code. If you really master it, it can even become an art. The best way to learn is by doing it, learning from others, and getting regular feedback on your code.

This chapter is not a simple 'x steps to success' guide. It is a collection of good practices and guidelines which you can implement in your own work. Do not try to implement all at once; pick one or two practices at a time and see how they work for you. Over time, your coding skills will improve. But before we start, we need to know what we aim for: what is good code?

## Writing clean, efficient, maintainable code

What is good code? Good code is code that is easy to read and
understand. A useful metric to evaluate code is the 'time till
understanding': how long does it take for your colleague to read
through your code and understand what it does  @boswell_Foucher
To understand code means:

- You can make changes.
- You can spot errors or inconsistencies.
- You can extend or reuse the code for new use cases.
- You understand how this code interacts with other code.

Writing better code means minimizing the 'time till understanding.' When
it is good enough is a matter of definition. In theory, it means that
the metric is equal to the time needed for a single, top-to-bottom
read-through of the code. In practice, this is not always possible,
because some code is inherently complex. Actually measuring the time
till understanding is also not recommended, because it will vary a lot
between different people with different expertise levels. It is, however,
a good goal to keep in mind, both when writing and reviewing code.


## Applying style guides and conventions

The easiest part of writing good code is applying a style guide to
your code. A style guide is a set of rules about how to format your
code. It includes things like indentation, spacing, line breaks, naming
conventions, and other aspects that contribute to the overall readability
of the code.

Examples of widely used style guides include the [tidyverse
style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/) for R and [PEP
8](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/) for Python. These guides are often
extended with local style guides, which may include conventions on file
naming, folder structure, and other institute-specific rules.

For most generic style guides, linters are available. Linters are tools
that can be integrated into your code editor or IDE and automatically
check your code against the style guide, like an automated spelling
check for code. Most linters can also autoformat your code, so you do
not have to worry about the details yourself.

Examples of linters and formatters:

- R: `lintr`, `styler`
- Python: `pylint`, `black`, `flake8`

Editor integration:

- R: RStudio supports `lintr` and `styler` via the addins menu and project options.
- Python: Editors like VSCode, PyCharm, and JupyterLab support `pylint`, `black`, and `flake8` via extensions or built-in tools.

Example: Before and after formatting

Unformatted Python:

```python
def calc(x,y):return x+y
```

Formatted Python (PEP 8):

```python
def calc(x, y):
    return x + y
```

Unformatted R:

```r
calc<-function(x,y){x+y}
```

Formatted R (tidyverse style):

```r
calc <- function(x, y) {
  x + y
}
```

Working with a style guide and a linter can be hard in the beginning,
especially if you have been programming for some time using your own
code style. You have to 'unlearn' your old habits and get used to the
new style. While this can be frustrating at first, it will pay off
later because you will be producing more consistent code. If you and
your colleagues use the same style, it also means that it is easier to
read each other's code, reducing the 'time till understanding.'

### Good coding practices

#### Keep it small ✂️

A book is not written as a single huge chapter but is broken down into
smaller chapters and sections. The same holds for code. If you break down
your code into smaller chunks, scripts, or files, it becomes much easier
to read and understand. Especially if these chunks of code can also be
related to the conceptual model of your workflow (REF chap conceptual
model) If the reader knows the context of the chunk of code, it is much
easier to understand what it does.

Break your code into small, focused units.

- In R, use functions for repeatable tasks, and scripts for logical parts of your workflow.
- In Python, split your code into modules and functions, and use classes only if necessary.

Example: Python

```python
# Too much in one function (bad)
def analyze_data(df):
    # data cleaning
    df = df.dropna()
    # feature engineering
    df['ratio'] = df['x'] / df['y']
    # modeling
    model = LinearRegression().fit(df[['ratio']], df['outcome'])
    return model
```

```python
# Split into small functions (good)
def clean_data(df):
    return df.dropna()

def feature_engineering(df):
    df['ratio'] = df['x'] / df['y']
    return df

def build_model(df):
    return LinearRegression().fit(df[['ratio']], df['outcome'])
```

Example: R

```r
# Bad: all in one go
df <- read.csv("data.csv")
df <- df[!is.na(df$x) & !is.na(df$y), ]
df$ratio <- df$x / df$y
model <- lm(outcome ~ ratio, data = df)
```

```r
# Good: modularized
df <- read.csv("data.csv")
clean_data <- function(df) {
  df[!is.na(df$x) & !is.na(df$y), ]
}
feature_engineering <- function(df) {
  df$ratio <- df$x / df$y
  df
}
```


By breaking up your code into smaller pieces, it is also easier to
test and debug. If a bug occurs, you can isolate it to a specific
function or module, making it easier to fix. Also, it makes it easier
to reuse code in other projects or workflows. If you have a function
that does one thing well, you can use it in multiple places without
having to rewrite it.

#### Keep it simple 🧩

Often, you write a piece of code once, but it is read many times.
Therefore, it is important to keep your code simple and easy to read.
Simple code is easier to understand and easier to review by a
colleague. Also, it helps with maintaining and extending your code in
the future. If you have to make changes to your code, it is easier to
do if the code is easy to read. This reduces the chances of
introducing bugs.

Your code probably lives in a project that will change. New
requirements will come in, new data is addded, and new functions are
needed. This means that your code often have to change. Very abstract
constructs or clever tricks may be hard to understand. Creating a cool
one-liner may be fun, but it is not always the best solution and a
drag on the readability of your code.

As an example, look at the following code snippet in which we
calculate the mean of two groups in a dataframe.

```r
# Create data.frame:
#  - X: random groups 1 or 2
#  - Y: random values between 1 and 10
df <- data.frame(
  X = sample(1:2, 20, replace = TRUE),
  Y = runif(20, min = 1, max = 10)
)

# Calculate the everage of each group using a clever one-liner (bad)
aggregate(Y ~ X, data = df, FUN = mean)

# Calculate the average of each group using a clear and simple approach (good)
df |>
  group_by(X) |>
  summarise(mean_Y = mean(Y))

```

While both approaches give the same result, the second approach is
much easier to read and understand. It is clear what the code does,
and it is easy to modify if needed. 

Another example of unnecessary code complexity is the use of nested
structures. These structures often appear in the form of nested loops
or nested function calls, or nested if statement. Please look at the
following example.

```r
result <- summarise(
  group_by(
    filter(
      mutate(
        iris,
        SepalRatio = Sepal.Length / Sepal.Width
      ),
      Species != "setosa"
    ),
    Species
  ),
  AvgRatio = mean(SepalRatio)
) |> 
  mutate(
    RatioCategory = ifelse(AvgRatio > 2, "High", "Low")
  )

```

In this code a lot things happen. However, it is hard to read and
understand what is going on. It is better to break it up into smaller
pieces and use intermediate variables. This makes it easier to read
and understand what is going on. The following code snippet shows a
better approach.

```r
iris_with_ratio <- iris |>
  mutate(
    SepalRatio = Sepal.Length / Sepal.Width
  )

iris_filtered <- iris_with_ratio |>
  filter(
    Species != "setosa"
  )

ratio_summary <- iris_filtered |>
  group_by(Species) |>
  summarise(
    AvgRatio = mean(SepalRatio),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

result <- ratio_summary |>
  mutate(
    RatioCategory = ifelse(AvgRatio > 2, "High", "Low")
  )

```

The above code is much easier to read and understand. It is clear what
is going on, and it is easy to modify if needed. It is also easier to
debug if something goes wrong. If you have a bug, you can isolate it
to a specific step, making it easier to fix.

#### Don’t repeat yourself (DRY) 🔁

The principle of DRY, don't repeat yourself, is a fundamental principle
in software development. It is about reducing repetition or duplication
of code and your logic. When you repeat the same code many times, it
becomes harder to maintain. If you need to change a rule or a formula,
you must find and update every copy. This is error‑prone and makes your
script fragile. DRY helps you keep your code consistent, easier to read,
and simpler to modify.

For example, if you want to create multiple models with different
variables:

```r
data("iris")
model_petal_width <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Petal.Width, data = iris)
model_sepal_length <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Length, data = iris)
model_sepal_width <- lm(Petal.Length ~ Sepal.Width, data = iris)
```

If you want to change the formula, you must change it in three places.
If you forget to change it in one place, you will have inconsistent
models. In this case, it is better to create a function that takes the
variable as an argument and returns the model. This way, you only have
to change the formula in one place.

```r
create_model <- function(variable) {
  lm(Petal.Length ~ get(variable), data = iris)
}

model_petal_width <- create_model("Petal.Width")
model_sepal_length <- create_model("Sepal.Length")
model_sepal_width <- create_model("Sepal.Width")
```

Or, even better, you can use a for loop to create the models:

```r
variables <- c("Petal.Width", "Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")
for (var in variables) {
    create_model(var)
}

```

Another option, which is more functional, is to use `lapply` to create
the models. Look at the next code example. 

```r
variables <- c("Petal.Width", "Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")
models <- lapply(variables, function(var) {
  lm(Petal.Length ~ get(var), data = iris)
})
names(models) <- variables
```

Now go read the previous
paragraph about keeping things simple. While the `lapply` approach is
more functional, it is also harder to read for less experienced R
users. The for loop is more explicit and easier to understand,
although much slower than `lapply`. Keeping things simple and DRY can
be conflicting principles, the right solution is often a matter of
taste and experience. 

#### Single responsibility 🧑‍🔬

The single responsibility principle says that each function, module or
script should do one clearly defined thing, and do it well. While coding,
this means that when you read a function, you can explain its job in
one short sentence without using the words “and”.

For example, a good function might “compute summary statistics for
numeric columns”. A function that “reads a file _and_ cleans the data
_and_ fits a model _and_ saves a plot” is doing too many things at once.

While single responsibility is a good principle, it is not always easy
to apply. It requires you to think about the purpose of your code and
how to break it down into smaller pieces. For a function it is often
easy to apply single responsibility, but for a module or script it can
be more challenging. You have to think about the overall workflow and
how to break it down into smaller steps. Your conceptual model from
the [Conceptual Design](conceptual-design.html#conceptual-design)
chapter can help you with this.

There is no general rule for how small a function should be. It
depends on the context and the complexity of the task. When writing a
function, you can ask yourself the following questions:

Does it makes code easier to read? When a function has one clear task,
you can understand it faster. You do not need to keep track of many
different steps and side effects in your head. If you open a script and
see small functions with clear names, it is easier to follow the flow
of data.

Does it makes code easier to test? If a function does one thing, you
can write tests that check that one behaviour. When something breaks,
you know which part to test and fix. If a function does many 
tasks, it becomes hard to write good tests and hard to know which part
is failing.

Does it makes code easier to reuse? A small function with a single
responsibility is simpler to use in a different project. You can take
that function and call it with new data. When functions combine many
steps, they are less flexible and harder to reuse.

Does it helps with debugging and maintenance? If a bug appears,
it is easier to locate it when each function handles one step. You can
add logging or print statements to a specific function and see where
things go wrong. In a big function with many responsibilities, the bug
can hide anywhere.

Does it supports change over time?. Requirements change. If each
responsibility is isolated in its own function or module, you can change
one part without touching the rest. This reduces the risk of breaking
other parts of the system.

If you can answer yes to most of these questions, you might consider
[refactoring](implementation-coding-standards.html#refactoring) your
code to follow the single responsibility principle more closely.

#### Naming functions and variables 🏷️

It is important to use meaningful names for variables and functions
because it makes your code easier to read and understand, both for
yourself and for others who may work with your code in the future. Clear
names describe what a variable represents or what a function does, which
helps prevent confusion and reduces the chances of making mistakes. Good
naming also makes it easier to maintain and update your code over time.

For example, consider the following code snippet:

```r
# Bad naming
x <- 10
y <- rnorm(x)
my <- function(y) {
  mean(y)
}

# Good naming
num_samples <- 10
random_values <- rnorm(num_samples)
calculate_mean <- function(values) {
  mean(values)
}
```

Also consider the 'scope' of the variable and where it is used in the
code. If the definition of the variable is 'close' to where it is
used, it is easier to understand what it represents. If the variable
is defined far away from where it is used, it can be harder to
understand its purpose. For example, when using a for loop, it is
often not necessary to provide a meaningful name for the loop
variable, because it is only used within the loop.

```r
for i in 1:10 {
  print(i)
}

```

In the above example it is clear that `i` is the loop variable and it
is only used within the loop. But if the loop is spread over many
lines of code, it can be helpful to give the loop variable a more 
meaningful name, like `sample_index` or `iteration_count`. This make
is easier to recognize the purpose of the variable and its role in the
loop.

How you write a variable name is also important. It is a good practice
to use a consistent naming convention throughout your codebase. This
makes it easier to read and understand your code, and it helps prevent
confusion. Some common naming conventions include:

 - snake_case: Words are all lowercase and separated by underscores (e.g., `my_variable`).
 - lowerCamelCase: The first word is lowercase, and subsequent words are capitalized (e.g., `myVariable`).  
 - UpperCamelCase: Each word is capitalized (e.g., `MyVariable`).  

Other conventions exists, but are not commonly used in R or Python,
for example:

 - kebab-case: Words are all lowercase and separated by hyphens (e.g.,
   `my-variable`). For R and Python, this is not a common convention,
   because hyphens are not allowed in variable names (it would be
   interpreted as a minus sign).
 - Hungarian notation: Prefixes indicate the type of variable (e.g.,
   `strName` for a string, `intCount` for an integer). This is also not
   commonly used in R or Python.

The best naming convention is the one that is most commonly used,
preferable one that is based on a common style guide:

  - [PEP 8 – Python Style Guide](https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/)
  - [tidyverse Style Guide for R](https://style.tidyverse.org/)

#### Error handling 🚨

If you write code, you'll will encounter errors. Some errors are
expected, and some are unexpected. It is frustrating to get an error
message that is not helpful, or even worse, to get no error message at
all but just erroneous results. Robust code anticipates and handles
potential problems gracefully. Always check inputs, provide meaningful
error messages, and use built-in mechanisms to catch and handle
errors.

For example in R if you expect a numeric argument for a function,
the user may provide a character string instead. If you do not check
the input, the function may fail with an error message that is not
helpful. And often the user has no what went wrong or where to find
the problem. If you check the input of the function, you can provide a
meaningful error message that helps the user understand what went
wrong and how to fix it. For example:

```r
random_vals <- rnorm(100)

calc_max <- function(x) {
  if (!is.numeric(x)) {
    stop("calc_max: Input must be numeric")
  }
  max(x)
}

```

If something unexpected happens, it is often better to let the error
propagate and crash the program, rather than silently failing or
returning incorrect results. This way, the user is immediately aware
that something went wrong and can take action to fix it. Also, the
user can catch these errors and handle them gracefully, rather than
having to deal with incorrect results later on. See the two code examples below for python and R.

```python
def safe_divide(a, b):
    """
    Divides a by b, raising a ValueError if b is zero.

    Parameters:
        a (float): Numerator
        b (float): Denominator

    Returns:
        float: Result of division

    Raises:
        ValueError: If b is zero.
    """
    if b == 0:
        raise ValueError("b cannot be zero")
    return a / b

# Using try/except to handle the error
try:
    result = safe_divide(10, 0)
except ValueError as e:
    print(f"Error: {e}")
```


```r
#' Safely divide two numbers
#'
#' Divides a by b and throws an error if b is zero.
#'
#' @param a Numerator.
#' @param b Denominator.
#' @return Result of division.
#' @examples
#' safe_divide(10, 2)
#' tryCatch(safe_divide(10, 0), error = function(e) print(e$message))
safe_divide <- function(a, b) {
  if (b == 0) stop("b cannot be zero")
  a / b
}

# Using tryCatch to handle the error, printing a message instead of crashing the program
tryCatch(
  safe_divide(10, 0),
  error = function(e) message("Error: ", e$message)
)
```


Don't forget to document your error handling in your function's
docstring or comments, so users know what to expect and how to handle
errors.

## Refactoring 🔄

Refactoring your code means improving the internal structure of your
code without changing its output or behaviour. It is a key software
engineering practice for keeping your code readable, maintainable, and
efficient. You refactor your code, for example, when the person
reviewing your code suggests improvements, or when you notice that
your code is getting messy and hard to read. Refactoring can involve
renaming variables, breaking down large functions into smaller ones,
removing duplicate code, or reorganizing the code structure. The goal
is to make your code cleaner and easier to understand, while
preserving its functionality.

Refactoring should always be supported by tests to
ensure you do not introduce errors. If you have an test that checks
the current behaviour of your code, you can run it after refactoring
to make sure everything still works as expected. If the tests pass,
you can be confident that your refactoring did not break anything.

Also, when refactoring, one must also thing about the documentation.
If you change the structure of your code, you may also need to update
the documentation to reflect the new structure. This includes updating
docstrings, comments, and any external documentation that references
the code.

- Do not refactor without tests: Before refactoring, write unit tests (REF chapter testing & validation) that cover current code behaviour.
  - Python: Use [pytest](https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/) or [unittest](https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html).
  - R: Use [testthat](https://testthat.r-lib.org/).
- Refactor in small steps: Make one logical change at a time and run your tests frequently.
- Keep commits focused for `git`: Each commit should address a single change, making it easier to track and revert if needed.
- Document refactoring: Note significant refactoring in your CHANGELOG and, if needed, in code comments.

## Reviewing 👀👀

No code should be used without being reviewed by a colleague. Code
review is an essential part of the software development process,
ensuring that code meets quality standards, is maintainable, and is
free of errors. It also promotes knowledge sharing among team members.

While code review can be done in many ways, the most common approach
is to use version control systems like Git, along with platforms like
GitHub or GitLab, which provide tools for pull requests (PRs) or merge
requests (MRs). These platforms allow developers to submit their code
changes for review, where colleagues can comment, suggest
improvements, and approve the changes before they are merged into the
main codebase.

When reviewing code, reviewers can focus on many aspects. For example:
 - Is the code clear and easy to understand?
 - Does it follow the team's coding standards and style guides?
 - Is the code well-documented, with comments and docstrings where necessary?  
 - Are variable and function names meaningful?
 - Does the code produce the expected results and handle edge cases?
 - Are there any potential bugs or performance issues?  

When asked for a review, it is good to know what kind of feedback the
author wants. If it is a first prototype, the autthor may want feedback
on the overall approach, readability, and design choices. Correct
functionality may not be the main concern at this stage. When the code
is published, one may want feedback on the documentation, especially
by someone outside the project.

Whatever the stage of the code, or the requested feedback. There is
always one aspect that should be taken into account: The code must be
clear and easy to understand. This is the most important aspect of
code review. If the code is not clear, it is hard to review and hard
to maintain. The code should be clear enough that a colleague can
understand it without having to ask the author for explanations.

While code review is dependent on the context of the project and the
team, there are some general guidelines that can help make the process
more effective:

 - _Step 1_: Focus on the 'time to understand' of the code. If it
   takes too long to understand or if you need to ask the author for
   explanations, the code is not clear enough. Discuss with the author
   how to make it clearer. This may involve refactoring, adding
   comments, or improving naming conventions.
 - _Step 2_: This is related to step 1. If you can understand the code,
   is it also readable? This sounds a bit strange, but an experienced
   programmer can read code that is not clear, but it is not easy to
   read. Readable code means that you can read it without having to
   think too much about it, that names of variables and functions are
   meaningful, and that the code is structured in a way that makes
   sense. Also the comments in the code should be clear and helpful.
   If you have to read a comment twice, it is not good. Also check for
   the coding style. If the code is not consistent with the style
   guide of the team, it should be reformatted.
 - _Step 3_: Check for correctness. Does the code do what it is supposed
   to do? Are there any bugs or errors? What happens if the code is
   used in a different context? Or with different data? (or even
   erroneous data?). Report any issues to the author and suggest
   improvements.

Additional steps can be added to the review process, depending on the
context of the project. For example, the review can focus on
performance, security, or scalability. Also, specific reviews can be
requested for certain parts of the code, such as tests. Or a broader
review can be requested where an experienced colleague looks at the
correct implementation of an algorithm or mathematical model, and discuss this
with someone who is experienced with the code.

### Giving feedback

When giving feedback, it is important to be constructive and
respectful. Your review is a way to help your colleague improve their code
and coding skills, not to criticize or judge them personally. Focus on
the code, not the person. Use specific examples and provide suggestions
for improvement. Avoid vague comments like "this is bad" or "this is
confusing." Instead, explain why something is problematic and how it
can be improved. If you have no clue how something can be improved, or
you can not pinpoint a certain bug, just be honest and say that you do
not know. When discussing these points with the author, you may come
up with a solution together.

Especially when you are very experienced with coding, it is easy to
forget that not everyone has the same level of experience. You may
have a lot of knowledge about a specific topic, but your colleague may
not. When giving feedback, it is important to consider the experience
level of the author and adjust your feedback accordingly. If you are
unsure, then note your feedback for yourself and offer to discuss this
face to face with the author. This way, you can provide feedback which
is more targeted at the experience level of the author. 

Be careful with 'normative' feedback. Code is like writing and
talking. Everybody has their own style and way of doing things. Even
if you apply a style guide, there are often many ways to implement a
solution. There is no single correct way to write code. If you have a personal opinion
about a specific coding style, it is important to be aware of this and
not impose your opinion on others. Instead, use your feedback as a
learning opportunity and discuss the pros and cons of different
approaches.

### Using code review tools

Code review means having a colleague look at your code before it is merged, to catch mistakes, improve code quality, and share knowledge. Most teams use pull/merge requests in GitHub or GitLab for review.

- Peer review: Submit a Pull Request (GitHub) or Merge Request (GitLab) with your changes. Assign a colleague as a reviewer.
- Request Guides:
  - [GitHub (Pull request)](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/proposing-changes-to-your-work-with-pull-requests/about-pull-requests)
  - [GitLab (Merge Requests)](https://docs.gitlab.com/user/project/merge_requests/)
- Automate checks: Use CI/CD pipelines to run automated style checks and tests.
- Use a checklist: Review for clarity, correctness, code style, documentation, and test coverage.

Example: Review Workflow in GitLab/GitHub

- Push your feature branch.
- Open a Merge Request (MR) or Pull Request (PR).
- Assign reviewers.
- Reviewers comment, request changes, or approve the MR/PR.
- Automated tests run via CI/CD (GitLab Runners/GitHub Actions).
- Merge once approved and tests pass.

See also the the [Turing Way guide in Code
Review](https://book.the-turing-way.org/reproducible-research/reviewing/).

## Structuring codebase (modules, scripts, notebooks)

Organize your project into logical modules, scripts, and notebooks. Make sure the structure matches your workflow and conceptual model. This makes it easier to reuse and maintain code.

- R: Use R projects or R packages for larger analyses.
- Python: Use packages (folders with `__init__.py`) or modules for reusable code.

A clear structure helps:

- Keep raw and processed data separate from code.
- Reuse scripts and functions in multiple analyses.
- Collaborate with others by making navigation intuitive.

In many projects it is helpful to have one “master script” (or
“do‑it‑all” script) that runs the full analysis pipeline by
calling smaller, focused scripts or functions (e.g. `01_load_data.R`,
`02_clean_data.R`, `03_analyse.R`, `04_plot_results.R`). This makes
it clear how to reproduce the complete workflow and where to look for
each step.
